description: Heart structure, pulmonary and systemic circulation, blood vessels and key cardiac definitions.
content_html:
The Double-Circulatory System

The cardiovascular system uses a double-circulatory system. This means blood makes two separate loops before returning to its starting point. The pulmonary circulation carries deoxygenated blood from the right side of the heart to the lungs, where carbon dioxide is released and oxygen is collected, before returning the now-oxygenated blood to the left side of the heart. The systemic circulation then carries that oxygenated blood from the left side of the heart out to every organ and muscle in the body, returning deoxygenated blood to the right side of the heart via the veins. Separating these two loops prevents oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood from mixing, ensuring maximum efficiency of oxygen delivery to the working muscles.

The Heart: Structure and Function

The heart is a hollow, muscular organ roughly the size of a fist, located in the chest slightly left of centre behind the sternum. It is divided into four chambers by a central wall called the septum. The two upper chambers are called atria (singular: atrium) — the right atrium receives deoxygenated blood returning from the body, and the left atrium receives oxygenated blood returning from the lungs. The two lower chambers are called ventricles — the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs, and the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood to the rest of the body. The left ventricle has a thicker, more muscular wall than the right because it must generate much higher pressure to push blood all the way around the body.

Valves inside the heart prevent the backflow of blood. The bicuspid valve sits between the left atrium and left ventricle. The tricuspid valve sits between the right atrium and right ventricle. The semilunar valves are located at the exit of each ventricle, where the aorta leaves the left ventricle and where the pulmonary artery leaves the right ventricle. All three sets of valves open due to changes in blood pressure and close automatically to maintain one-directional blood flow.

Key Fact

Blood pathway: vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → semilunar valve → pulmonary artery → lungs (gas exchange) → pulmonary vein → left atrium → bicuspid valve → left ventricle → semilunar valve → aorta → body. Note that the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood — this is the opposite of most arteries.

The Pathway of Blood Through the Heart

Following the pathway of blood precisely is a common exam demand. Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium via the vena cava. From the right atrium it passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. The right ventricle contracts and forces blood through the semilunar valve into the pulmonary artery to the lungs. In the lungs, carbon dioxide is released and oxygen is picked up by haemoglobin in the red blood cells. The now-oxygenated blood returns to the heart via the pulmonary vein, entering the left atrium. It passes through the bicuspid valve into the left ventricle, which contracts powerfully, ejecting oxygenated blood through the semilunar valve into the aorta — from which it is distributed to every organ and muscle in the body.

The Role of Red Blood Cells

Red blood cells are the oxygen-carrying cells of the blood. They contain haemoglobin — a red iron-containing protein that binds readily with oxygen in the oxygen-rich environment of the lungs to form oxyhaemoglobin. When red blood cells reach the working muscles, where oxygen concentration is low, oxyhaemoglobin breaks down and releases its oxygen into the muscle tissue. The same red blood cells then pick up carbon dioxide — a waste product of respiration — and carry it back to the lungs to be exhaled. Without red blood cells in sufficient numbers, oxygen transport collapses and athletic performance is severely impaired.

Blood Vessels: Arteries, Veins and Capillaries

Arteries carry blood away from the heart. They have thick, muscular walls because they must withstand the high pressure generated by ventricular contraction. The walls are elastic, allowing them to stretch and recoil with each heartbeat, smoothing out blood flow. All arteries (except the pulmonary artery) carry oxygenated blood.

Veins carry blood back towards the heart. They have thinner walls than arteries because blood pressure is much lower. Veins contain valves that prevent backflow, which is especially important in the legs where blood must travel upward against gravity. All veins (except the pulmonary vein) carry deoxygenated blood.

Capillaries are the microscopic vessels that form the link between arteries and veins in the tissues. Their walls are just one cell thick, allowing oxygen and nutrients to diffuse into the muscle cells and carbon dioxide and waste products to diffuse back into the blood. Every working muscle is surrounded by a dense network of capillaries. Long-term aerobic training increases capillary density in muscles, improving oxygen delivery.

One of the most common errors in cardiovascular questions is stating that the pulmonary artery carries oxygenated blood. It does not. The pulmonary artery is the only artery in the body that carries deoxygenated blood — it takes blood from the right ventricle to the lungs specifically so that oxygen can be collected. Similarly, the pulmonary vein is the only vein that carries oxygenated blood — returning fresh blood from the lungs to the left atrium. The rule “arteries carry oxygenated blood” has two exceptions that you must memorise: the pulmonary artery (deoxygenated away from heart) and the pulmonary vein (oxygenated toward heart).

Cardiac Output, Stroke Volume and Heart Rate

Three linked measurements describe how efficiently the heart pumps blood. Stroke volume is the amount of blood pumped out of the heart with each beat. At rest, stroke volume is approximately 70 ml. Heart rate is the number of beats per minute (bpm). A typical resting heart rate is 60–80 bpm (trained endurance athletes may have a resting heart rate as low as 40 bpm — a long-term adaptation called bradycardia). Cardiac output (Q) is the product of the two:

$$Q = \text{stroke volume} \times \text{heart rate}$$

At rest: Q = 70 ml × 72 bpm = 5,040 ml/min (approximately 5 litres per minute). During intense exercise, heart rate can rise to 200 bpm or more and stroke volume increases to around 110–130 ml, so cardiac output can reach 20–25 litres per minute in a trained athlete.

Key Fact

Cardiac output (Q) = stroke volume × heart rate. Always show the formula, substitute the values, and include the unit (ml/min or L/min). Example: Q = 70 ml × 72 bpm = 5,040 ml/min. At maximum exercise this can rise to over 20,000 ml/min in a trained athlete.

During exercise, the working muscles need much more oxygen and glucose than at rest. The body redistributes blood flow so that a greater proportion of cardiac output goes to the active muscles. Blood supply to the digestive system and other non-essential organs is reduced, while blood flow to the working skeletal muscles and heart muscle increases dramatically. This redistribution is an important short-term effect of exercise. It explains why exercising vigorously immediately after a large meal can cause discomfort — the digestive system is competing with the muscles for blood supply at a time when the muscles' demands are greatly elevated.
exam_tip_html: The cardiac output calculation is one of the most predictable questions in this topic — always worth attempting. Show three things: (1) the formula (Q = stroke volume × heart rate), (2) the substitution with figures from the question, and (3) the answer with the correct unit (ml/min or L/min). Missing the unit is a frequent error that costs the final mark. On a ‘Describe the pathway of blood’ question, a common mistake is to say the pulmonary artery carries oxygenated blood — it is the one artery in the body that carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs. OCR also requires you to name the bicuspid, tricuspid and semilunar valves and place them correctly in the blood pathway — not just state that “valves prevent backflow.” For the 8-mark Evaluate question, ensure your argument covers both sides: address what happens when the cardiovascular system functions efficiently and consider what happens when it is under stress, linking both to the specific sporting context given.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The cardiovascular system uses a double-circulatory system: pulmonary circulation (heart ↔ lungs) and systemic circulation (heart ↔ body). Blood pathway: vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → semilunar valve → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → bicuspid valve → left ventricle → semilunar valve → aorta → body.
  • Red blood cells carry oxygen (bound to haemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin) to the working muscles and transport carbon dioxide back to the lungs for removal.
  • Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate (approximately 5 L/min at rest; up to 25 L/min during maximal exercise in a trained athlete). During exercise, blood flow is redistributed to the working muscles.

practice_questions.text: Name the vessel that carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying cardiac output as the total volume of blood pumped by the heart per minute; 1 mark for stating it is calculated as stroke volume multiplied by heart rate (or giving the formula Q = SV × HR).

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows data for a trained cyclist at rest and during a 20-minute time trial.

Condition      | Heart rate (bpm) | Stroke volume (ml)
At rest        | 48               | 85
During race    | 172              | 115

Calculate the cardiac output at rest and during the time trial. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct resting cardiac output with working shown: Q = 48 × 85 = 4,080 ml/min; 1 mark for correct exercise cardiac output with working shown: Q = 172 × 115 = 19,780 ml/min; 1 mark for including correct units (ml/min or equivalent L/min) on both answers. If method is correct but arithmetic is wrong, award 1 mark for the correct formula and substitution.

practice_questions.text:
A 16-year-old club swimmer's heart rate data is recorded during a training set. Resting: 62 bpm. End of warm-up: 105 bpm. Peak (mid-set): 178 bpm. Five minutes after finishing: 88 bpm.

Interpret what the data tells you about how the cardiovascular system responds during and after the swim set.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the increase in heart rate from rest to peak (116 bpm rise) and stating that this reflects the increased demand for oxygen from the working muscles; 1 mark for explaining that stroke volume also increases during exercise, meaning cardiac output rises substantially; 1 mark for identifying the recovery drop (from 178 bpm to 88 bpm within 5 minutes) and linking this to the body's return towards its resting state; 1 mark for a valid sporting interpretation (e.g. the large rise in heart rate confirms the high oxygen demand of competitive swimming; the drop in recovery heart rate suggests the swimmer is reasonably well conditioned). If calculations are used, show working and units.

practice_questions.text: Explain the role of the bicuspid, tricuspid and semilunar valves in the pathway of blood through the heart.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining the tricuspid valve: located between the right atrium and right ventricle; prevents blood flowing back from the right ventricle into the right atrium; 1 mark for explaining the bicuspid valve: located between the left atrium and left ventricle; prevents backflow from the left ventricle into the left atrium; 1 mark for explaining the semilunar valves: located at the exit of each ventricle (into the aorta and pulmonary artery); prevent backflow into the ventricles between beats; 1 mark for correctly placing all three in the sequence of blood flow through the heart. Accept equivalent anatomical descriptions.

practice_questions.text: A county-level middle-distance runner is preparing for a 12-week pre-season training block. Evaluate the importance of an efficient cardiovascular system to her performance in a competitive 800 m race, considering both heart structure and the pathway of blood.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Full range of relevant cardiovascular content applied consistently to 800 m racing. Includes: double-circulatory system (pulmonary and systemic loops) enabling continuous oxygen delivery; named valves preventing backflow ensuring one-directional flow; cardiac output calculation linked to exercise demand (heart rate and stroke volume both rising during the race); red blood cells transporting oxygen to the quadriceps and gastrocnemius during the race effort; redistribution of blood flow to working muscles; long-term training adaptations (cardiac hypertrophy, increased stroke volume, lower resting heart rate) that improve efficiency. Evaluation includes both sides: the value of a highly efficient cardiovascular system vs the constraints (genetic ceiling on maximum cardiac output; lactic acid accumulation in the final stages regardless of cardiovascular fitness). Justified conclusion about whether cardiovascular efficiency is the most important limiting factor for 800 m performance. Consistent sporting application throughout.

Secure (5-6 marks): Most cardiovascular structures and responses covered with reasonable accuracy; applied to the 800 m context; evaluation of at least two relevant points; conclusion reached; some minor inaccuracies or undeveloped sections.

Developing (3-4 marks): Cardiovascular structures described with limited application to the 800 m race; cardiac output mentioned but not calculated or applied; one-sided.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about heart rate increasing during exercise; limited structure or sporting application.

Cardiac output = stroke volume ÷ heart rate
Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate
Cardiac output = heart rate ÷ stroke volume

knowledge_checks.q: The _____ is the muscular wall that divides the left and right sides of the heart.
The double-circulatory system consists of the pulmonary circulation and the _____ circulation.
Match each blood vessel to its description:
right: Carry blood away from the heart under high pressure
Return blood to the heart; contain valves to prevent backflow
One-cell-thick vessels allowing gas exchange with tissues

flashcard_questions.q: What does the double-circulatory system mean?
flashcard_questions.a: Blood passes through the heart twice per circuit: once via pulmonary (heart-lungs) and once via systemic (heart-body).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of the tricuspid valve?
flashcard_questions.a: Prevents blood flowing back from the right ventricle into the right atrium.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of the bicuspid valve?
flashcard_questions.a: Prevents blood flowing back from the left ventricle into the left atrium.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of the semilunar valves?
flashcard_questions.a: Prevent blood flowing back into the ventricles from the aorta and pulmonary artery between beats.

flashcard_questions.q: Which vessel carries deoxygenated blood FROM the right ventricle TO the lungs?
Which vessel carries oxygenated blood FROM the lungs TO the left atrium?
What is the role of red blood cells in the cardiovascular system?
flashcard_questions.a: They carry oxygen (bound to haemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin) to the muscles and CO2 back to the lungs.

flashcard_questions.q: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate. What is the unit?
Calculate cardiac output: stroke volume 70 ml, heart rate 72 bpm.

flashcard_questions.a: The volume of blood ejected by one ventricle per heartbeat (in ml).

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the left ventricle have a thicker wall than the right?
flashcard_questions.a: It must generate greater pressure to pump blood around the whole body via the systemic circulation.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to blood flow distribution during exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: Blood is redistributed to working muscles; supply to non-essential organs (e.g. digestive system) is reduced.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do arteries have thick, elastic walls?
flashcard_questions.a: To withstand and smooth out the high-pressure pulse of blood from the ventricle.
To prevent backflow of blood, especially in the legs where blood flows against gravity.

glossary_terms.definition: A system in which blood passes through the heart twice per complete circuit: once through the pulmonary loop (heart to lungs) and once through the systemic loop (heart to body).
The muscular wall that divides the left and right sides of the heart, preventing oxygenated and deoxygenated blood from mixing.
The valve between the left atrium and left ventricle; it has two flaps and prevents blood flowing backwards into the atrium when the ventricle contracts.
The valve between the right atrium and right ventricle; it has three flaps and prevents backflow from the ventricle to the atrium.
Half-moon-shaped valves at the exit of each ventricle (into the aorta and pulmonary artery) that prevent blood flowing back into the heart between beats.
The vessel carrying deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs for gas exchange.
The vessel that carries oxygenated blood from the lungs back to the left atrium of the heart.
The large vein that returns deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium of the heart.
The largest artery in the body, carrying oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the rest of the body.
The volume of blood ejected by one ventricle in a single heartbeat, measured in millilitres (ml).
The number of times the heart beats per minute (bpm).
The total volume of blood pumped by one ventricle per minute; calculated as stroke volume multiplied by heart rate.
